Performance & Scalability Benchmarks

Source: vignettes/benchmarks.Rmd
benchmarks.Rmd

Executive Summary

Small Area Estimation often involves large administrative registries or extensive spatial networks with hundreds or thousands of domains. Traditional implementations in R often rely on interpreted loops, pure R Fisher-scoring routines, or large memory allocations for D×DD \times D dense covariance matrices.

fastsae fits the frequentist models in compiled C++ (RcppArmadillo; sparse Cholesky factorisations for the SAR models) and the Bayesian models with INLA. At n=1,000n = 1,000 domains:

  • Fay-Herriot: 1,250x faster than sae and 21,071x faster than emdi.
  • Spatial Fay-Herriot: 46x faster than sae and 49x faster than emdi.
  • Spatio-Temporal Fay-Herriot (T=5T = 5, point estimates): 29x faster than sae.

Benchmark Results Table

Model (n=1,000n = 1,000 domains, 5 covariates) fastsae sae emdi
Fay-Herriot 0.000639 s (1.91 MB) 0.799 s (39.0 MB; 1,250x slower) 13.5 s (222 MB; 21,071x slower)
Spatial Fay-Herriot 0.518 s (78.7 MB) 24.1 s (239 MB; 46x slower) 25.2 s (310 MB; 49x slower)
Spatio-Temporal FH (T=5T = 5), point estimates 39.8 s (495 MB) 1160 s (3.60 GB; 29x slower) -

Times are medians of bench::mark(). The frequentist rows were measured on 2026-10-26 with fastsae 1.0.0, sae 1.3 and emdi 2.2.3 on the same simulated data sets (Apple M4, R version 4.6.1 (2026-06-24); benchmarks/bench_frequentist.R), each in its own R process; memory is the increase of the peak resident memory of that process during the fits, which includes memory allocated by compiled code (increases of a few tens of MB vary from run to run and should not be compared). ‘sae’ has no analytical MSE for the spatio-temporal model, so that row compares point estimates; with its analytical MSE, fastsae took 39.3 s. The Bayesian fastsae rows were re-measured on 2026-10-14 (benchmarks/bench_bayes_fastsae.R), the tipsae rows (4 chains of 2,000 iterations) come from an earlier run on the same data.

Architectural Insights: Why is fastsae so Fast?

  1. Compiled C++ Linear Solvers: Instead of interpreting nested loops in R, fastsae implements Fisher scoring and the analytical MSE in Armadillo C++. The spatial Fay-Herriot model never forms a D×DD \times D inverse: with A=(I−ρW′)(I−ρW)A = (I - \rho W')(I - \rho W) and M=A+σ2E′Ψ−1EM = A + \sigma^2 E'\Psi^{-1}E, V−1V^{-1}, g1,…,g4g_1, \dots, g_4 and the kriging terms follow from sparse Cholesky solves with AA and MM (Eigen, AMD ordering).

  2. Zero-Copy Matrix Operations: Memory allocations for large intermediate structures (VV, V−1V^{-1}, PP) are avoided or reused across Fisher iterations rather than reallocated on the heap.

  3. OpenMP Multi-Threaded Bootstrap: Bootstrap resampling runs natively in parallel across CPU cores using #pragma omp parallel for, avoiding the serialization overhead of R worker processes (parallel::makeCluster / foreach).

  4. Woodbury Identity for Panel Data: In eblup_stfh, inversion of the block (DT×DT)(DT \times DT) covariance matrix VV is reduced to operations on individual D×DD \times D and T×TT \times T blocks via Kronecker and Woodbury decomposition, transforming an O((DT)3)O((DT)^3) bottleneck into scalable O(D3+T3)O(D^3 + T^3) steps.

  5. Integrated Nested Laplace Approximations (INLA): For complex hierarchical generalized and spatio-temporal models (hb_area), fastsae utilizes INLA to compute analytical posterior margins directly from sparse Gaussian Markov Random Fields, bypassing Monte Carlo sampling entirely.

Bayesian Spatio-Temporal Benchmark: fastsae (INLA) vs tipsae (Stan MCMC)

To assess Bayesian small area estimation performance, fastsae::hb_area() was benchmarked against tipsae::fit_sae(), the state-of-the-art Stan MCMC package for spatio-temporal Beta small area models.

The test used the official tipsae panel dataset: emilia (38 health districts in Emilia-Romagna over 5 years, N=190N = 190 domains ×\times years) with spatial polygon contiguity matrix WW from emilia_shp.

Metric tipsae::fit_sae (Stan MCMC) fastsae::hb_area (INLA)
Model Beta, Besag ICAR + domain-specific RW(1) family = "beta", spatial = "besag", temporal = "rw1", st_interaction = "domain-specific"; same structure, different priors
Computation Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (NUTS) Integrated nested Laplace approximation (INLA’s default "compact" mode for Beta)
Execution time 22 min (4 chains x 10,000 iterations with 2,000 warm-up, in parallel; largest R̂\hat R 1.007). Every transition reaches the maximum tree depth; 4 chains x 2,000 iterations (120 s) have not converged (R̂\hat R 1.07, and 1.12 on a Linux runner) 1.1 s
Posterior means vs converged tipsae Reference r=0.999r = 0.999, mean absolute difference 0.0017 (largest 0.006)
Posterior SD vs tipsae Reference ratio 0.81 to 1.22 (the priors differ)

Measured on 2026-10-16 (tipsae reference refitted on 2026-10-17) on one machine (Apple silicon, R 4.6.1, INLA 26.8.7, tipsae 1.0.3); times depend on the hardware. INLA needs no chains or warm-up, but its fit should still be checked (convergence, from INLA’s mode search).

Agreement with Stan MCMC (Beta model, n=1,000n = 1,000)

To check that the speed of fastsae::hb_area does not come at the cost of its estimates, both packages were fitted with their defaults to the n=1,000n = 1,000 data set of the Beta benchmark (independent area effects, sampling variances from the direct estimates; benchmarks/bench_beta_concordance.R). The two packages do not fit identical models (their priors differ, and fastsae fixes the precision at a first-stage estimate while tipsae makes it a function of the model mean), so the comparison is between what a user obtains from each package:

Metric fastsae::hb_area (INLA) tipsae::fit_sae (Stan)
RMSE against the true area means 0.0678 0.0684
Coverage of the 95% intervals 93.3% 91.1%
Mean width of the 95% intervals 0.252 0.259
Time 4.3 s 184 s

The posterior means of the two packages differed by 0.0096 on average (absolute difference), and the posterior SDs of fastsae were 0.99 times those of tipsae in the median area (90% of the areas between 0.88 and 1.17). The largest R̂\hat{R} of the tipsae fit was 1.008.
